questions.question: The three Indian growing seasons are Kharif, ____ and Zaid.
A small hand-hoe used for digging and weeding is called a ____.
A layer of dry leaves on the soil is called ____.
A seed needs moisture, warmth and ____ to germinate.
Unwanted plants that take water and nutrients from your crops are called ____.
What is a kitchen garden? List THREE benefits of having one at school.
questions.answer: A kitchen garden is a small garden where you grow plants you can eat — vegetables, herbs, sometimes fruits. Three benefits: (i) fresh, safe food full of nutrients; (ii) hands-on learning of planning, observation and care; (iii) attracts bees and butterflies for pollination and makes the school greener and cooler. (Also: shared harvests build friendship.)

questions.question: Name the three growing seasons in India and give one example crop for each.
questions.answer: (i) Kharif — sown in June/July with the monsoon. Examples: gourds, brinjal, beans. (ii) Rabi — sown in October/November. Examples: spinach, coriander, peas. (iii) Zaid — sown in March/April. Examples: cucumber, watermelon.

questions.question: List FIVE simple tools / materials needed for a kitchen garden and what each is used for.
questions.answer: (i) Khurpi — small hand-hoe for digging and weeding. (ii) Trowel — for transplanting seedlings. (iii) Watering can — to water plants gently. (iv) Compost — to mix with soil for nutrients. (v) Mulch (dry leaves) — to keep soil moist and weed-free. (Also: rake, gloves, stakes, seeds, pots.)

questions.question: Explain the three main ways to start a plant.
questions.answer: (i) Direct sowing — put the seed straight into the bed; works for spinach, coriander, radish. (ii) Seedlings — start seeds in a small tray, then transplant the small plants into the bed; works for tomato, brinjal, chilli. (iii) Cuttings — take a piece of stem from a plant and put it in moist soil to grow roots; works for mint and curry leaves.

questions.question: List FOUR everyday-care steps for kitchen-garden plants.
questions.answer: (i) Water early morning or late afternoon, not at noon, and only if the soil is dry. (ii) Weed once a week, pulling weeds out by their roots. (iii) Mulch with dry leaves to keep the soil moist and cool. (iv) Watch for pests; pick caterpillars off by hand or use mild neem-water. (Also: stake tall plants like tomato and brinjal; keep a garden diary.)

questions.question: How would you harvest (a) spinach, (b) radish, (c) tomato? Explain in one line each.
questions.answer: (a) Spinach — pick large outer leaves, leaving the plant to keep growing. (b) Radish — pull up the whole plant when the root is firm. (c) Tomato — pluck the fruit when it is ripe (right colour, firm but not hard).
questions.explanation: Different methods for leaf, root, fruit.

questions.question: Your school has a small empty plot of about 5×5 m. Plan a Rabi kitchen garden for it. Describe: (i) which crops you will grow and why, (ii) where you will place each, (iii) what tools you will use, (iv) one risk you must plan for.
questions.answer: (i) For a Rabi season (October–February) plot of 5×5 m I will grow spinach, coriander, peas, radish and a few coriander/mint pots — all easy short-cycle crops, suited to the cool months and providing a mix of leaves, pulse and root for the school kitchen. (ii) Place tall pea plants on the north side so they don't shade smaller plants; spinach and coriander in long rows in the middle; radish in a short row in front (south side). Leave a one-foot path between rows. Mint goes in pots so it doesn't spread everywhere. (iii) Tools — khurpi for digging, trowel for transplanting, a watering can for gentle watering, a small rake, gloves and wooden tags for row labels. Soil mixed with compost (2:1). (iv) Risk: caterpillars eating leaves. Plan: check leaves twice a week, pick caterpillars by hand, plant marigolds at the corners as a natural deterrent, keep a small bottle of neem-water spray ready.
questions.explanation: Full plan with crops, layout, tools and risk.

questions.question: After two weeks of caring for your kitchen garden, you find that some leaves have small holes and the soil is dry every morning. What might be wrong and what would you do? Use ideas from the chapter.
questions.answer: Two problems: (1) holes in leaves suggest pests, most likely caterpillars or aphids. (2) Dry soil every morning suggests not enough watering, or watering at the wrong time. Action plan: (a) Inspect leaves carefully — turn them over and look for caterpillars, eggs or aphids; pick caterpillars off by hand; spray a mild neem-water solution; plant marigolds nearby for the future. (b) Water early morning so the soil stays moist through the day; touch the soil before watering — if it is already moist, skip; mulch with dry leaves to lock in moisture. (c) Record both problems and the steps taken in the garden diary so I can see if they help over the next week. Reflection turns problems into learning.
